To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the subjective knowledge people report to have about their odor-naming knowledge is not as accurate as the subjective knowledge people claim to have about their person-name knowledge.

the subjective knowledge people possess about their own odor knowledge is characterized by (1) a high degree of certainty that the name is on the tip of the tongue and (2) an inability to retrieve the name.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the metacognitive processes involved in naming odors, and the paper provides evidence that the metacognitive judgements of FOK and TOT are not as useful in odor naming as they are in other memory domains.
the subjective knowledge that people have about their own memory for odor and person information, and how this knowledge can be used to improve the retrieval of odor names.
the subjective knowledge people possess about their own memory and the way this knowledge is used to guide retrieval attempts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our inability to name odors is not due to the fact that odors are difficult to name, but rather that they are difficult to identify.
odor naming is not a problem of memory, but a problem of metamemory.
the difficulty in naming odors is not due to poor associations, but rather to the poor identification of the odor, that is, to the poor knowledge 'what it is'.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the difficulties in odor naming are primarily due to failures to know 'which' odor it is, and that the FOK and TOT experiences are not very different for odors as compared to other types of stimuli, and are not particularly informative about the likelihood of later successful odor naming.

our subjective knowledge of what we can do with odors is not as poor as often assumed, and that our inability to name odors is not due to a uniquely poor association between an odor's name and the odor itself.
our inability to name odors is due to failures to know 'which it is' (i.e., to identify the odor) rather than failures to know 'how to name' the odor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people have a very poor subjective knowledge about their actual odor-naming abilities, and that this subjective knowledge is not a good predictor of actual performance.

the difficulties people experience when trying to name common odours is not a problem of the odour itself, but rather a problem of how people perceive and remember odours, which are not perceived and remembered as easily as other sensory stimuli, such as visual or verbal stimuli.
odor-naming failures are not due to the lack of associations between the odors and their names, but to a more general lack of information about odors and their properties.
